why_this_tool: Every piece of the GPU stack plugs into Kubernetes primitives (the kubelet device plugin API, extended resources, labels, taints and DRA claims), so practising those primitives on a local cluster teaches what the vendor stack automates even without a GPU.
alternatives: NVIDIA GPU Operator installs driver, container toolkit, device plugin, feature discovery and DCGM Exporter in one Helm release instead of by hand; the standalone k8s-device-plugin covers only advertising and time-slicing or MPS config; a DRA GPU driver replaces counted resources with claims; managed cloud node pools hide the whole stack; Slurm or Ray schedule GPUs outside Kubernetes.

setup.do: Install kubectl and start a local multi-node cluster with kind or minikube, with one control plane and two workers.
setup.done_when: kubectl get nodes lists three nodes in Ready state.
setup.why: Every later step needs a cluster with more than one node, so that scheduling choices between a device node and a plain node are visible. A local cluster costs nothing and needs no GPU.

setup.do: Check that the Dynamic Resource Allocation API groups are served by your cluster version, and enable them if they are not.
setup.done_when: Listing DeviceClasses returns an empty list rather than an unknown resource error.

source.title: Set Up DRA in a Cluster | Kubernetes

setup.why: The sharing and partitioning steps later use DRA objects, which only exist when the API is enabled. Finding this out now avoids a confusing failure halfway through.

setup.do: Install an example DRA driver that publishes simulated devices, as the local substitute for a real GPU driver.
setup.done_when: Listing ResourceSlices shows simulated devices published for at least one worker node.

source.title: Set Up DRA in a Cluster | Kubernetes

setup.why: A laptop has no GPU, so a simulated driver stands in for the vendor one. It publishes devices through the same API a real GPU driver uses.

steps.do: Read how a device plugin registers with the kubelet and advertises devices as an extended resource.
steps.done_when: You can draw the chain from pod to scheduler to kubelet to device plugin to runtime to driver, and say what each layer adds.
steps.why: This is the layer that makes Kubernetes aware of GPUs at all. Driver, container toolkit and runtime sit below it, and the scheduler only sees what the plugin reports.

steps.do: Run a check of which container runtime each node uses and confirm it is containerd and healthy.
steps.done_when: The wide node listing shows containerd as the runtime on every node and all nodes are Ready.

source.title: Changing the Container Runtime on a Node from Docker Engine to containerd | Kubernetes

verified.section_found: Verify that the node is healthy

steps.why: The container toolkit works by reconfiguring the node runtime so containers can see the device. You need to know which runtime the kubelet talks to before reasoning about that layer.

steps.do: Deploy a sample device plugin as a DaemonSet on one worker; with no GPU, use one of the listed example plugins that advertises a fake device.
steps.done_when: Describing the worker node shows the new extended resource under Capacity and Allocatable with a non-zero count.
steps.why: Running the plugin as a DaemonSet is how the real GPU plugin is deployed. Watching a new resource appear on the node shows the advertising mechanism directly.

steps.do: Create a pod that requests one unit of the advertised extended resource in its container limits.
steps.done_when: The pod is Running on the worker that has the plugin, and the node description shows one unit allocated.
steps.why: This is how a workload asks for a GPU: a whole-number limit on a vendor resource name. The scheduler then places the pod only on a node that advertises it.

steps.do: Create a second pod that asks for more devices than exist, save both pod objects to files, and compare their status fields.
steps.done_when: You can point to the Unschedulable condition and its message in the pending pod and to the Ready condition in the running one.
steps.why: Saved pod objects are the record you compare when a GPU workload will not start. The status conditions say whether the cause is scheduling, admission or the container itself.

steps.do: Read the vendor implementations section and map each GPU Operator component onto a piece you deployed by hand; installing the operator needs a real GPU node, so the sample plugin stays as the local substitute.
steps.done_when: You have a short table listing each operator component, the layer it covers, and what you did manually in its place.
steps.why: The operator bundles driver, toolkit, device plugin, feature discovery and monitoring into one install. Knowing the manual equivalent of each makes operator failures much easier to debug.

steps.do: Label the device node with a made-up accelerator model and schedule a pod onto it with a node selector, copying what automatic node labelling does.
steps.done_when: The pod lands on the labelled node, and changing the selector to a model that does not exist leaves a new pod Pending.

verified.section_found: Manage clusters with different types of GPUs

steps.why: Feature discovery labels nodes with GPU model and memory so workloads can pick the right hardware. Doing it by hand shows what those labels are for.

steps.do: Configure a NoSchedule taint on the device node and add a matching toleration only to the pods that request the device.
steps.done_when: A plain pod with no toleration never schedules onto the tainted node, while the device pod with the toleration still runs there.
steps.why: GPU nodes are costly, so ordinary pods must be kept off them. A taint plus toleration is the standard way to dedicate nodes with special hardware.

steps.do: Create a DeviceClass and a ResourceClaimTemplate for the simulated devices, then run a workload that references the claim.
steps.done_when: A ResourceClaim generated for the pod shows as allocated and reserved, and the pod is Running.

source.title: Allocate Devices to Workloads with DRA | Kubernetes

steps.why: DRA is the newer way to request GPUs. A claim describes the device you need by attributes rather than by count, which is what makes flexible sharing possible.

steps.do: Read how DRA models partitionable devices, then note which sharing mode each maps to: MIG as partitions, time-slicing and MPS as shared access to one device; these modes need real GPU hardware, so the simulated driver is the local substitute.
steps.done_when: You can state for time-slicing, MPS, MIG and DRA what is isolated, what is shared, and how a pod asks for it.
steps.why: Sharing a GPU is a trade between isolation and density. Seeing how partitions are modelled in the API explains why MIG gives hard isolation while time-slicing and MPS do not.

steps.do: Reproduce the whole flow on a freshly created cluster from saved manifests only, in the order the DRA user workflow describes.
steps.done_when: After deleting and recreating the cluster, applying the manifest directory alone brings the device pod and the claim-based pod to Running.
steps.why: A platform engineer delivers GPU setup as versioned manifests, not as a sequence of typed commands. Rebuilding from files proves nothing depended on manual state.

steps.do: Configure least-privilege RBAC for the DRA driver service account, following the node-local driver pattern, and re-run the claim workload.
steps.done_when: The claim-based pod still reaches Running, and an access check shows the driver account cannot update claim status for other nodes.

source.title: Hardening Guide - Dynamic Resource Allocation | Kubernetes

steps.why: On a shared production cluster a device driver runs on every node with access to claim status. Restricting its permissions limits the damage from a compromised node.
